Owner Decides To Sell His 1957 Chevy Bel Air That Has an Incredible Number on the Clock
44 photos
Photo: eBay seller jalle9209
What’s the first thing you typically think of when seeing a 1957 Bel Air ? For me, it’s the mystery of what’s hiding under the hood, as the final year of the Tri-Five era represented Chevrolet’s big foray into the V8 space.
This Bel Air is here to remind us about all of these. The car is being presented as a survivor, and while it only takes a few seconds to figure out that this isn’t necessarily accurate, it’s still a very intriguing classic car.
One of the main selling points is undoubtedly the mileage. The owner reveals that his “very clean survivor” has only 21,406 miles on the clock, and this is the original mileage. It’s almost too good to be true, especially because this car is 69 years old, meaning that it was driven for only approximately 300 miles every year.
This car has certainly spent an important part of its life inside, which kind of explains why it received several important upgrades and a transmission rebuild.
Photo: eBay seller jalle9209 There’s a good reason why I said that engines are the first thing I always think of whenever I come across a 1957 Bel Air. Chevrolet used this model year to introduce the 283 Turbo-Fire, an iconic engine for the GM brand that ended up making its way to almost every single nameplate in its portfolio.
The full-size family used the 283 as the base V8 for nearly one decade, and this made perfect sense. The 283 delivered a good balance of efficiency and performance, so many buyers who ordered a full-size Chevrolet didn’t feel the need for an upgrade under the hood.
The 283 was obtained by boring out the 265 to a higher displacement. The 283 joined the Bel Air lineup with a two-barrel configuration and a single exhaust, offering 185 horsepower in the lowest output setup.
If customers wanted more power, they could go for the Super Turbo-Fire 283, which replaced the two-barrel carburetor with a four-barrel and the single-exhaust system with a dual exhaust. The output was more impressive, as this upgraded 283 delivered 220 horsepower.
Chevrolet didn’t stop here, and another 283 version pushed the output to 245 horsepower thanks to dual four-barrel carburetors. A fuel-injected version served as the top configuration, using solid lifters to produce 283 horsepower.
Photo: eBay seller jalle9209 There’s a good reason why this 1957 Chevy Bel Air could end up catching the attention of so many people online. It’s not fitted with a two-barrel 283 but with a four-barrel setup rated at 245 horsepower. This is the most powerful non-fuel-injected 283 for the 1957 model year, and while no actual production numbers are available, it goes without saying that not many of these ended up seeing the daylight.
The owner says this is the original engine that came with the car when it rolled off the assembly line, and it is paired with a Turboglide automatic transmission that has already been rebuilt.
Otherwise, from a mechanical perspective, the car is in tip-top shape, albeit this is also the place where it steps away from that survivor promise. It boasts an upgraded stainless exhaust system, upgraded power brakes, a racing tachometer, a high-performance cooling fan, and a B&M shifter.
The cabin has also received some extra touches, so you’ll get a custom plus interior that should feel quite nice but is not original.
Photo: eBay seller jalle9209 Sure, this 1957 Chevy Bel Air is no longer original, but it’s honestly difficult to find a very good reason to step away. The mileage is something you see every day, and considering the car was born and raised in California, the rust invasion has never been a problem.
My recommendation is simple: call the seller and ask all your questions before you agree on a visual inspection. This Bel Air might be advertised as a survivor, but it has already received touches that push it away from this otherwise fantastic condition, so you need to see everything with your eyes before making an offer.
You still have enough time to do it, considering the listing will continue to be up for several more weeks - assuming the car doesn’t find a buyer in the meantime.
Photo: eBay seller jalle9209 As for the price, the original engine and the low miles are the things that make the car more expensive than many other 1957 Bel Airs.
The owner believes $40,000 is a fair price, but they also enabled the Make Offer option, just in case someone wants the car but doesn’t want to pay that much for it. 30 people have already added the vehicle to their watchlists, but it’s unclear if anyone is involved in talks regarding a possible purchase.
As for live verifications, you can find this car parked in Hinckley, Illinois, where it’s obviously tucked away to avoid any unnecessary problems that would end up altering its beautiful shape.
